Dealing with a power cut on your aquarium

facts.fact: A top-mounted trickle (wet/dry) filter sits on top of the aquarium; it is the less common placement compared with sumps below the tank.
In a top-mounted trickle filter, water is pumped up onto perforated trays and trickles through them, so the filter wool stays wet but is not fully submerged.
Bacteria in the filter oxidise ammonia to nitrite and then to nitrate; nitrate still builds up, so regular partial water changes are needed.
Bacterial colonies take weeks to establish, so a new tank stocked too fast risks 'new tank syndrome'.
Water dribbling through bioballs in a trickle section becomes well aerated.
Keepers describe an overhead wet/dry as working like a standard wet/dry, but without drilling the tank; one argues it loses less flow to pump head.
A typical layout starts with a mechanical pre-filter: polyester floss in a holed tray about two inches deep.
In one keeper's overhead design, filter fluff goes in the first drawer and bio media in the drawers after it; the drilled drawer bottoms act as drip plates.
To spread water evenly, holed pipes can be laid one every 3–4 inches over the polyester: 1/8" holes every 3" on the bottom, two rows of 3/16" holes every 2" on the sides, 3/8" holes every 1" on top.
One keeper returns the output through a spray bar near the water surface, which he expected to be quiet.
Too few holes in the drip tray cause overflow; too many leave water spread unevenly over the media.
Getting an even trickle without channeling or overflow is often very difficult in wet-dry filters.
Aquarium Science rates a wet-dry filter at about 70% as efficient as a static, submerged bioball filter, and a 100% bioball wet-dry sump at about 10% of a fluidised-bed K1 sump.
Aquarium Science calls submerged bioballs a poor medium and suggests static K1 media and 20 ppi foam after the trickle stage instead.
Keepers report that noise mostly comes from the trickle section; one runs a 2000 GPH overhead filter and finds it tolerable, and another said 300 GPH should not be too loud.
In a power cut, beneficial bacteria start dying once water has stopped flowing through the filter for roughly an hour.
During a power cut, a battery-powered air pump keeps fish supplied with oxygen; putting the filter's bio media in the tank above the airstone may keep the bacteria alive.
Aeration matters more after a few hours of outage, especially in warm or heavily stocked tanks.
Clean the pump impeller chamber regularly: limescale and grime can stop the impeller restarting after a power cut even though it runs fine while powered.
After power returns, check that the filter has actually restarted; an unnoticed failure can cause serious problems.
After a long outage, rebuilding the bacterial colony can take weeks; lightly stocked tanks cope better.
Vietnamese hobbyists call this filter 'lọc tràn trên', as opposed to 'lọc tràn dưới'.

Vietnamese names for the parts include máng lọc tràn trên (tray, 3–5 compartments), máy bơm chìm (submersible pump), ống dây dẻo (flexible hose), bông lọc trắng (white floss), tấm bùi nhùi (scouring pad), sứ lọc (ceramic media), đá nham thạch (lava rock), san hô vụn (crushed coral) and than hoạt tính (activated carbon).

Vietnamese names for the compartments include ngăn lọc thô (coarse/mechanical), ngăn lọc vi sinh (biological) and ngăn lọc hấp thụ (chemical/absorption); zeolite and UV lamps (đèn tia UV) are also used.

Kits sold in Vietnam include the BAOYU G30 (3 chambers, tanks up to 40 cm, 3 W, 220 L/h), G50 (4 chambers, up to 50 cm, 3 W, 220 L/h) and G60 (up to 60 cm, 6 W, 300 L/h); the pump is included but the media is not.
Vietnamese shops also sell Yee-branded top filters, filter floss (bông lọc) and ceramic rods (thanh sứ) for biological filtration.
